title: Can, must, want, may
goal: Use the five helper verbs behind almost every request, permission and obligation — and know the difference between *nie musisz* and *nie możesz*.
bekal: asking for help and permission politely

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Możesz mi pomóc?
dialogs.intro: The dorm kitchen, late afternoon. Ania sits in front of her laptop looking desperate.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Muszę napisać podanie, ale nie umiem pisać oficjalnie.
lines.id: I have to write an application, but I can't write formally.
lines.literal: I-must write application, but not I-know-how write formally.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mogę spróbować, ale nie jestem pewny.
lines.id: I can try, but I'm not sure.
lines.literal: I-can try, but not I-am sure.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: Want a coffee? We can sit here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Chętnie. Tylko muszę wyjść o piątej — mam zajęcia.
lines.id: Gladly. But I have to leave at five — I have class.
lines.literal: with-pleasure. only I-must leave at fifth — I-have classes.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Zdążymy. Czy mogę pożyczyć twój słownik?
lines.id: We'll make it. Can I borrow your dictionary?
lines.literal: we-will-manage. whether I-can borrow your dictionary?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Proszę. Ale nie wolno w nim pisać.
lines.id: Go ahead. But no writing in it.
lines.literal: please. but not allowed in it write.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Nie będę. A wolisz herbatę czy wodę?
lines.id: I won't. Would you rather have tea or water?
lines.literal: not I-will. and you-prefer tea or water?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wolę wodę. Nie muszę pić kawy, żeby myśleć.
lines.id: I'd rather have water. I don't need coffee to think.
lines.literal: I-prefer water. not I-must drink coffee, so-that think.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Umiesz pisać po polsku szybciej niż ja!
lines.id: You write Polish faster than I do!
lines.literal: you-know-how write in-Polish faster than I!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie przesadzaj. Trzeba jeszcze wszystko sprawdzić.
lines.id: Don't exaggerate. It all still needs checking.
lines.literal: don't exaggerate. needed still everything check.

notes: **The second verb is always in the dictionary form.** *Muszę napisać*, *mogę spróbować*, *chcesz jeść*. Just like English "must write" or "can try" — and you never need a "to".

**Możesz mi pomóc?** is the most common way to ask for help. The more polite version: *Czy mógłbyś mi pomóc?* (m) / *Czy mogłabyś…?* (f) — a conditional form you can memorize whole for now, without unpacking the rules.

**Móc and umieć are not the same.** *Móc* = can because circumstances allow it (*mogę przyjść jutro* — I can come tomorrow). *Umieć* = can because you have the skill (*umiem gotować* — I can cook). Choosing the wrong one changes the meaning, not just the tone.

**Nie muszę is not nie mogę.** *Nie muszę pić kawy* = I **don't have to** drink coffee. *Nie mogę pić kawy* = I **can't / mustn't** drink coffee. It's the same distinction as English *don't have to* vs *can't*, and beginners mix them up just as often.
**Nie wolno** means "not allowed" as a general ban, with no subject: *Tu nie wolno palić* (no smoking here). It pairs with *można* (you may) and *trzeba* (you need to, you must).
**Żeby** means "so that, in order to" and takes the dictionary form when the subject is the same: *Piję kawę, żeby myśleć.* When the subject changes, the form is different — that's for A2.

**Szybciej niż ja** — "faster than me". Comparatives are made with the ending *-iej / -ej*: *szybko → szybciej*, *dobrze → lepiej*, *dużo → więcej*. The last three are irregular — and, of course, the most common.

**Nie przesadzaj** — a negative command: *nie* + the command form. The full command forms come in A2, but a few you'll hear all the time are worth learning now: *proszę poczekać* (please wait), *nie martw się* (don't worry), *chodź* (come on).

grammars.title: Five helper verbs
body: All of them take the dictionary form, and three are irregular — so this table is worth learning whole.
after: Look at *móc*: *g* changes to *ż* in the four middle forms (*mogę* but *możesz*). It's the same kind of switch as *iść → idę / idziesz* in unit 5.
*Chcieć* and *woleć* are often used directly with a noun, with no second verb: *Chcę kawę* (I want coffee), *Wolę herbatę* (I prefer tea). The noun takes the object form.
⚠️ When ordering, *chcę* sounds demanding. Use *poproszę* (unit 8) in shops and restaurants, and save *chcę* for chatting with friends.

grammars.title: Sentences with no subject: trzeba, można, wolno
body: Three words that make a sentence apply to anyone — like the "must", "may" and "no…" of English public signs.

head: Word
English
Example
Translation
rows: You need to buy a ticket.

after: All of them take the dictionary form and **never change form** — there's no *trzebam* or *możny*. Six words, zero extra memorizing.
*Czy można…?* is the safest way to ask a stranger for permission: it's polite without making you choose between *ty* and *pan*.

blocks.title: Saying no without sounding rude
items: Put *niestety* (unfortunately) in front of a refusal — it softens almost any sentence.
Give a short reason: *Niestety nie mogę, mam zajęcia.* Poles don't expect long excuses, but a bare no feels cold.
Offer an alternative: *Może jutro?* (How about tomorrow?)

blocks.text: Subjectless sentences are everywhere in Polish public spaces. Learn to recognize them once and you'll never have to guess again.

blocks.title: The two words most easily confused
items: ***Wejście*** (entrance) and ***wyjście*** (exit) differ by one letter, and misreading them is the classic tourist mistake at Polish stations.
Remember them by the prefix: *w-* like "in", *wy-* like "out". The same prefixes work in the verbs: *wchodzić* (go in), *wychodzić* (go out).
